passage: In the reception classroom, Mridul was fitting the last piece into his farm puzzle when Sumit shouted and snatched it from his hand, catching his wrist. Mridul's stomach dropped and he felt very small. His fist curled to hit back, but he stopped. "Stop, that hurts," he said, his voice wobbling. He stepped away and walked quickly to the teacher's desk. "Sumit grabbed me." The teacher came over and crouched between the two boys.

qa.q: What did Sumit snatch from Mridul's hand?
qa.a: He snatched the last piece of the farm puzzle.

qa.q: How was Mridul feeling when Sumit shouted and grabbed him?
qa.a: He felt scared and small, and his wobbly voice and dropped stomach show it. He also felt an urge to hit back.

qa.q: Why was stepping away and fetching the teacher a good choice?
qa.a: Hitting back would probably have made the fight bigger. Saying "stop, that hurts" and getting a trusted adult let the problem be sorted out fairly.

qa.q: How might Sumit have been feeling when he grabbed the piece?
qa.a: He probably wanted the piece badly and could not wait, and may have been angry or upset. He was probably surprised when Mridul stayed calm and went to get help.

grounding: A friend shouts or grabs and I feel scared and small; a wise child says stop, steps back and fetches a teacher.

passage: Under the neem tree beside the village school, Abhinav rolled the wooden bullock cart along the dust to the fence and back. Yusuf sat waiting, hands tucked under his knees. Then Abhinav stopped and held the cart out. "Ab tumhari baari." Yusuf blinked. A warm, surprised feeling spread through his chest. He pushed the cart slowly. The next day he ran it along the fence once and held it out to Abhinav. "Ab tum."

qa.q: Where did Abhinav roll the wooden bullock cart?
qa.a: Abhinav rolled it along the dust to the fence and back, under the neem tree.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when Abhinav held the cart out to him?
qa.a: He was surprised and warm inside. His blink and the warm feeling in his chest show he had not expected to be given a turn.

qa.q: What did Yusuf learn from being given a turn that he then put into practice?
qa.a: He saw that fair sharing feels good, so the next day he gave Abhinav a turn after his own. 😊

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel when Yusuf holds the cart out to him?
qa.a: Abhinav likely feels happy that the kindness was returned, and that it started a fair back-and-forth between them.

grounding: Another child hands me the toy after a turn; I feel warm and surprised and later offer my own turn.

passage: Note from the class teacher. Yesterday Vishal and Usha argued over the puzzle. This morning Vishal sat apart with crossed arms, watching Usha build with blocks. At snack he told me, "I am still cross with her. But I want to play blocks." I did not push him to make up. After a while he walked over, held out a block and said, "Okay, let's play again." Usha took it, and I noticed his shoulders loosen. I will keep an eye on it.

qa.q: What did Vishal hold out to Usha?
qa.a: He held out a block.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Vishal have about Usha at snack time?
qa.a: He was still cross with her but missed playing and wanted to join the blocks.

qa.q: What did the teacher do well by not forcing Vishal to make up?
qa.a: They let him get there in his own time, since holding a grudge for a while is normal at this age. A gentle nudge worked better than force.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt when Vishal held out the block?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and glad to have her friend back, and took the block to show she was ready to play.

grounding: After a fight the child is still cross but misses playing, and offering a block is a brave step.

passage: Note from Afreen and Jagdish's after-school carer. At four o'clock Jagdish took the toy train his sister Afreen was using. Her face went red and her hand shot up as if to pinch him. She stopped, clenched her fist and shouted, "Didi! Jagdish took my train!" I came over and asked each to speak in turn. Afreen said, "He can have it after I finish the track." Jagdish agreed. She still glared at him, but she stayed beside him at the track.

qa.q: What did Jagdish take from Afreen?
qa.a: He took the toy train Afreen was using.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when her hand shot up and then she clenched her fist?
qa.a: She was furious and wanted to win, but she also loves her brother, so she held back from pinching.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that was a wiser choice than pinching?
qa.a: She called the carer and, once asked, suggested turns: he can have the train after she finishes the track.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see the moment he took the train?
qa.a: He probably just wanted a turn and did not expect her fury. Being listened to in turn and getting the train after the track probably felt fair to him.

grounding: A sibling takes the toy I am using; I feel love and fury but call a grown-up and agree on turns.

passage: Monday: Madhav and Shankar both grabbed the toy drum. The teacher came, asked each to say what happened without interruption, then turned a sand timer over. "Shankar first, then Madhav." Madhav's shoulders relaxed. Wednesday: another tug-of-war over the spade. Madhav walked to the teacher himself. "Can you help us?" Friday: the boys turned the sand timer over on their own and waited, watching the sand fall.

qa.q: What did the teacher use to set turns with the drum?
qa.a: They used a sand timer.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel about the teacher stepping in on Monday?
qa.a: He felt safe, because someone fair was listening to both boys and nobody was called bad. His shoulders relaxing shows the relief.

qa.q: What did Madhav learn to do on Wednesday, and why does it work?
qa.a: He went to the teacher for help himself, since big problems can be handed to a fair adult without shame.

qa.q: How might Shankar see the teacher's way of handling Monday?
qa.a: He probably felt heard and treated equally, since he was asked to speak first and had a turn with the drum.

grounding: The teacher listens to both children and sets turns with a timer; the child learns to trust a fair adult with big problems.

passage:
"Hansa, why aren't you eating?"
"I forgot my biscuits."
"Look, I have two." Santosh snapped his biscuit in half. "You have this one."
"Really? All of it?"
"Half is yours. Half is mine." He grinned. "My tummy feels nice."
The teacher, passing, smiled. "That was kind, Santosh. You can keep your other half."
"I know!" He crunched happily.

qa.q: What did Santosh do with his biscuit?
qa.a: He snapped his biscuit in half and gave half to Hansa.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling after he shared the biscuit?
qa.a: He felt proud and warm, as his grin and "My tummy feels nice" show.

qa.q: How did the teacher respond wisely to Santosh's sharing?
qa.a: They praised the kindness but told him he could keep his other half, without pushing him to give away everything. 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Hansa when she had no biscuits and Santosh offered half?
qa.a: Hansa was probably hungry and a little surprised, since she asked "Really? All of it?" It let her join in at snack time.

grounding: I break my biscuit and give half to a friend who has none; I feel proud and warm, and the kindness is chosen, not forced.

passage: Tuesday: Uma opened her school bag and her tiffin was not there. She stared at her desk, tummy rumbling. Jaya slid half her paratha across. Uma felt happy and a little shy. She whispered "Thank you" and took only that half. Wednesday: Uma checked her tiffin twice at home before leaving. Friday: she tucked an extra laddu in her box and, at lunch, offered it to Jaya with both hands.

qa.q: What was missing from Uma's school bag on Tuesday?
qa.a: Her tiffin was not there.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when Jaya slid half her paratha across?
qa.a: She felt happy and a little shy. Her whispered thanks and taking only the half she was offered show both.

qa.q: What did Uma do afterwards that keeps the kindness going?
qa.a: She planned ahead by packing an extra laddu on Friday and offering it to Jaya. Taking more than was offered would have spoiled it. 😊

qa.q: How might Jaya feel when Uma offers the laddu with both hands?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and touched that her kindness was remembered, and glad to see Uma being generous back.

grounding: A friend shares her tiffin when mine is forgotten; I feel happy and shy, say thank you and share back another day.

passage: I am Reena and I live upstairs from Joseph. Last Sunday his mother told him, "Give your red racing car to Kiran right now." Joseph went stiff and pulled the car to his chest. "No! It's mine!" His face looked angry, or maybe puzzled, I cannot tell. His mother crouched. "You can keep the red one special. Pick another to share." He thought, went to his box and came back with a plastic truck.

qa.q: Which toy did Joseph's mother ask him to give to Kiran?
qa.a: She asked him to give his red racing car.

qa.q: What might Joseph have been feeling when he pulled the car to his chest?
qa.a: He looked angry and maybe confused, because it was his favourite thing. Reena says it is hard to be sure what he felt.

qa.q: How did Joseph's mother's second sentence help more than her first?
qa.a: She let him keep the special car and gave him a choice to pick another toy, so sharing came from him.

qa.q: How might Reena's view of the scene differ from Joseph's experience of it?
qa.a: Reena only saw his stiff body and words, so Reena guesses. Joseph knows how much the red car mattered and how forced sharing felt.

grounding: A parent says give it now before I am ready; I am angry and confused, and a better way lets me keep one special and pick another.

passage: Monday: Lokesh saw Baljeet's shiny pencil box with stars on the lid, and his tummy hurt. He turned away and coloured hard. Wednesday: at home, he told his mother, "I wish I had a box like Baljeet's." She nodded. "That is a big wish." Friday: at school he took a breath. "Baljeet, can I hold it for a turn?" Baljeet passed it over. Lokesh held it carefully, and the ache in his tummy eased a little.

qa.q: What was on the lid of Baljeet's pencil box?
qa.a: There were stars on the lid.

qa.q: What did Lokesh's tummy ache tell you about how he felt on Monday?
qa.a: It suggests a strong envy, a wanting so big that it hurt. He turned away and coloured hard to cope with it.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that helped, compared with hiding or lying about it?
qa.a: He named the wish to his mother and then asked Baljeet for a turn. Saying the feeling openly is a better route than hiding it.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Lokesh's request on Friday?
qa.a: Baljeet may feel pleased or proud of the box and see the polite request as a fair one. Passing it over shows he is willing to share.

grounding: I see a classmate's shiny box and want it so much my tummy hurts; envy is normal and I name it and ask for a turn.

passage: Tuesday: Sonali counted the orange slices. "Saurabh has more! Not fair!" She cried and pushed her plate away. Wednesday: their father said, "One cuts, the other chooses." Saurabh cut the paratha carefully and Sonali chose, still peering at both halves. Friday: it was Sonali's turn to cut. She measured with her eyes, tongue out, then looked up at her brother. "You choose." Saurabh picked, and she pressed her lips together but did not cry.

qa.q: What did Sonali count on Tuesday?
qa.a: She counted the orange slices.

qa.q: Why did Sonali cry "Not fair!" on Tuesday?
qa.a: Fairness matters hugely to her, and she saw that her brother had more. She may also have felt sad and left out.

qa.q: How does the rule from their father help a fair split?
qa.a: When one cuts and the other chooses, the cutter has a reason to make the halves even, and both children can trust the result. 🙂

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh to cut when Sonali is watching so closely?
qa.a: He may feel the pressure of being watched, and know that she will check his work. Being careful about it is a way of showing he cares that it is fair.

grounding: I count who got the bigger piece and cry not fair; a family lets one cut and the other choose.
